1    Introduction
Let pn denote the n-th prime and define

                                       H1 := lim inf (pn+1 − pn ).                                    (1)
                                                n→∞

The twin-prime conjecture asserts that H1 = 2. It is a special case of the prime-tuple conjecture of
Hardy and Littlewood [HL23], which predicts infinitely many simultaneous prime values for every
fixed collection of shifts with no local congruence obstruction. The bounded-gap problem asks for
the weaker conclusion H1 < ∞. Its resolution has led to a quantitative problem: how small a
bound for H1 can be obtained from the distribution of primes in arithmetic progressions and the
choice of sieve weights?
    A finite set H := {h1 , . . . , hk } of distinct integers is admissible if its reductions modulo every
prime omit at least one residue class. Its diameter is diam(H) := maxi hi − mini hi . If infinitely
many translates n + H contain at least two primes, then H1 ≤ diam(H): the two primes enclose
a pair of consecutive primes with no larger gap. Thus a theorem giving two-prime translates for
every admissible k-tuple reduces the numerical gap problem to finding a short admissible tuple. The
number of shifts required by the sieve is therefore a central quantity in the successive improvements
of H1 .

Their sieve also showed that a level of distribution for primes strictly greater than 1/2 would imply
bounded gaps. The classical Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem reaches exponent 1/2, so this approach
required additional distributional information. Zhang [Zha14] obtained the necessary gain for a
restricted family of squarefree moduli composed of small prime factors and proved H1 < 7 × 107 .
The factorization of these moduli made stronger averaged estimates possible and supplied a way
to use distribution beyond the classical range in the sieve.
    Maynard [May15] introduced a multidimensional Selberg sieve, independently developed by
Tao, and proved H1 ≤ 600 using the Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem. The same method gives
bounded intervals containing any prescribed number of primes. Allowing the divisor attached
to each shift to vary independently turns the choice of weights into a variational problem in k
variables. D. H. J. Polymath [D. 14b] refined this problem by enlarging the support of the weights
and improving the finite variational calculation. The resulting theorem for 50 shifts, together with
an admissible 50-tuple of diameter 246, gives H1 ≤ 246. This bound also uses only Bombieri–
Vinogradov distribution.
    In parallel, D. H. J. Polymath [D. 14a] developed stronger equidistribution estimates for smooth
squarefree moduli, whose prime factors satisfy prescribed size bounds, and Stadlmann [Sta25]
further improved the available distribution range. Applying such estimates to prime gaps requires
control of the moduli produced by pairs of sieve divisors. An enlargement of the support improves
the resulting prime-gap bound only when the resulting divisor products retain the factorizations
needed by the distribution estimates. The support geometry and the modulus family must therefore
be considered together.
    Stadlmann [Sta26] combines a Bombieri–Vinogradov support region with a region adapted to
moduli having a large smooth factor. The mixed divisor products lead to relaxed equidistribution
estimates suited to this hybrid support. Together with a refined variational calculation, this gives
a theorem for 49 shifts and the bound H1 ≤ 240.
